--- title: "Job C — Generate Scenarios" subtitle: "RBIG backward to sample joint return scenarios" --- *Apply-the-tool track · Job C.* A risk model is only as good as the scenarios you feed it, and the dangerous scenarios are the **joint** ones — the days when many holdings crash at the same time. This lab runs Gaussianization in **reverse** as a scenario generator: fit RBIG forward so the data becomes a standard Gaussian (a tidy bell-shaped cloud), then draw fresh Gaussian points and push them back through the *inverse* map to get new return-like draws. The single fit-then-sample recipe is fixed on Rung 1 and reused unchanged as the data grows up under it — from a 2-D pair whose answer we know, to a real basket of stocks. **What you will produce:** a stress set — a batch of made-up joint scenarios whose co-crash structure (how often names crash together) matches the real book — ready to hand to the uncertainty module's risk calculations. --- ## 🧪 Rung 1 · Toy — Known Answer Start where the truth is not in doubt. `datasets.correlated_returns(rho=0.7)` draws a **known** 2-D Gaussian pair: the two assets move together with correlation $\rho = 0.7$, and each asset on its own (its *marginal*, the single-asset distribution) has variance one. Both numbers are baked into the generator, so we know them exactly. A scenario generator that is working must reproduce *both* — get the same correlation back and the same single-asset shapes — and here we can check each by hand. ::: {#9ae1097b .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} def correlation(z: Float[Array, "n 2"]) -> float: """Pearson correlation of two standardized columns. ρ = (1/n) Σₜ zₜ₀·zₜ₁ / (σ₀·σ₁) [dimensionless] For z-scored columns σ ≈ 1, so this is just the normalized gram entry. """ n: int = z.shape[0] zc: Float[Array, "n 2"] = z - z.mean(0) # mean-center each column gram: Float[Array, "2 2"] = einx.dot("n i, n j -> i j", zc, zc) / n # Σₜ zₜᵢ·zₜⱼ / n return float(gram[0, 1] / np.sqrt(gram[0, 0] * gram[1, 1])) # off-diagonal / √(σ₀²·σ₁²) x_toy, y_toy = datasets.correlated_returns(n=3000, rho=0.7, seed=0) X_toy: Float[Array, "n 2"] = np.column_stack([x_toy, y_toy]) X_toy = (X_toy - X_toy.mean(0)) / X_toy.std(0) # standardize → z-scores rho_true: float = correlation(X_toy) # ρ read straight off the generator print(f"X_toy: {X_toy.shape} known correlation ρ ≈ {rho_true:.3f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` X_toy: (3000, 2) known correlation ρ ≈ 0.707 ``` ::: ::: **The algorithm — fit forward, sample backward.** Gaussianization learns an invertible map $T$ with $T(\text{data}) \approx \mathcal{N}(0, I)$. Generating new data is then just the inverse map applied to fresh Gaussian noise: ``` fit T : data → z ~ N(0, I) # RBIG, forward sample z ~ N(0, I) # draw in the easy space generate x = T⁻¹(z) ~ data # inverse map → new data-like draws ``` `AnnealedRBIG.fit` learns $T$; `.sample(n)` does the draw-then-invert in one call. This is the *entire* generator — defined once here, reused on every rung: ::: {#8b54e2c6 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} from rbig import AnnealedRBIG def fit_generate(data: Float[Array, "n d"], n_gen: int, seed: int = 0) -> Float[Array, "n_gen d"]: """Fit RBIG forward (data → Gaussian), then sample its INVERSE map. T : data → z ~ N(0, I) learned by .fit (forward Gaussianization) x = T⁻¹(z), z ~ N(0, I) produced by .sample(n) (backward → new draws) """ model = AnnealedRBIG(n_layers=30, rotation="pca", random_state=seed).fit(data) return model.sample(n_gen) # (n_gen, d) fresh scenarios gen_toy: Float[Array, "n_gen 2"] = fit_generate(X_toy, n_gen=3000, seed=0) print(f"generated {gen_toy.shape[0]} scenarios with the same fit-then-sample recipe") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` generated 3000 scenarios with the same fit-then-sample recipe ``` ::: ::: Now read the generated draws against what we *know* is there — the correlation and the marginals: ::: {#eaa350a3 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} rho_gen: float = correlation(gen_toy) # ρ of the inverse-map draws print(f"correlation true {rho_true:+.3f} generated {rho_gen:+.3f}") print(f"marginal std true {X_toy.std(0).round(2)} generated {gen_toy.std(0).round(2)}") print(f"marginal mean true {X_toy.mean(0).round(2)} generated {gen_toy.mean(0).round(2)}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` correlation true +0.707 generated +0.700 marginal std true [1. 1.] generated [0.97 0.98] marginal mean true [ 0. -0.] generated [-0.01 -0.01] ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-toy-roundtrip .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, (ax0, ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 4.2)) for ax, data, col, ttl in [(ax0, X_toy, COOL, f"real · ρ = {rho_true:.2f}"), (ax1, gen_toy, WARM, f"generated · ρ = {rho_gen:.2f}")]: ax.scatter(data[:, 0], data[:, 1], s=8, c=col, alpha=0.3, edgecolors="none") ax.set_xlim(-4, 4) ax.set_ylim(-4, 4) ax.set_xlabel("asset 1 (z)") ax.set_ylabel("asset 2 (z)") ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=11) despine(ax) bins = np.linspace(-4, 4, 40) ax2.hist(X_toy[:, 0], bins=bins, density=True, color=COOL, alpha=0.55, label="real") ax2.hist(gen_toy[:, 0], bins=bins, density=True, color=WARM, alpha=0.55, label="generated") ax2.set_title("asset 1 marginal", fontsize=11) ax2.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False) despine(ax2) fig.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The known-answer round-trip. Left: the real ρ=0.7 cloud. Middle: RBIG-generated scenarios from the inverse map — same tilt, same spread. Right: the two marginal histograms of asset 1 overlaid; the generated marginal (orange) lands on the real one (blue). The generator reproduces both the correlation and the marginal shapes it was never told directly.](lab-jobC-scenarios_files/figure-html/fig-toy-roundtrip-output-1.png){#fig-toy-roundtrip width=1544 height=489} ::: ::: The known answer holds: the inverse map hands back the same $\rho \approx 0.7$ and the same Gaussian marginals. The recipe is correct — now we let the data get harder. --- ## 🎭 Rung 2 · Toy-Real — A Stylized Market A clean Gaussian pair never happens in markets. What *does* is a **co-crash**: two names that drift together on calm days and plunge together on the bad ones, with heavy tails (big losses happen more often than a Gaussian would predict) that a Gaussian sampler would shave off. `datasets.tail_dependent_pair()` is a simplified stand-in for that — a shared shock built from a fat-tailed Student-*t* distribution, so both assets get fat tails and tend to hit their worst days together. We run the **exact same** `fit_generate` and ask the question that matters: does the inverse map reproduce the lower-left corner where both assets crash at once — the structure a plain Gaussian simulation (a Monte-Carlo, meaning draws from random noise) would miss? ::: {#3a29bb26 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} a, b = datasets.tail_dependent_pair(n=2000, df=3, seed=0) X_pair: Float[Array, "n 2"] = np.column_stack([a, b]) # already standardized cc_real: float = cocrash_fraction(X_pair[:, 0], X_pair[:, 1]) # P(both in worst 10%) print(f"stylized co-crashing pair: {X_pair.shape} real co-crash = {cc_real:.0%}") gen_pair: Float[Array, "n_gen 2"] = fit_generate(X_pair, n_gen=2000, seed=0) # same recipe cc_gen: float = cocrash_fraction(gen_pair[:, 0], gen_pair[:, 1]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` stylized co-crashing pair: (2000, 2) real co-crash = 56% ``` ::: ::: A Gaussian fit to the same correlation is the benchmark to beat — it keeps the tilt but thins the tail, so its co-crash falls short of the real one: ::: {#89dd94e2 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} rho_pair: float = correlation(X_pair) # ρ of the fat-tailed pair rng = np.random.default_rng(0) g_pair: Float[Array, "n 2"] = rng.multivariate_normal( # Gaussian MC, same ρ [0, 0], [[1, rho_pair], [rho_pair, 1]], size=2000) cc_gauss: float = cocrash_fraction(g_pair[:, 0], g_pair[:, 1]) print(f"{'source':<22}{'co-crash':>10}") print("-" * 32) print(f"{'real pair':<22}{cc_real:>10.0%}") print(f"{'RBIG scenarios':<22}{cc_gen:>10.0%} ← inverse map keeps the joint tail") print(f"{'Gaussian MC (same ρ)':<22}{cc_gauss:>10.0%} ← thins it") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` source co-crash -------------------------------- real pair 56% RBIG scenarios 53% ← inverse map keeps the joint tail Gaussian MC (same ρ) 52% ← thins it ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-pair-cocrash .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13.5, 4.6), sharex=True, sharey=True) panels = [(X_pair, COOL, f"real · co-crash {cc_real:.0%}"), (gen_pair, WARM, f"RBIG scenarios · co-crash {cc_gen:.0%}"), (g_pair, "0.5", f"Gaussian MC · co-crash {cc_gauss:.0%}")] for ax, (data, col, ttl) in zip(axes, panels): qx, qy = np.quantile(data[:, 0], 0.10), np.quantile(data[:, 1], 0.10) # 10% crash lines box: Float[Array, "n"] = (data[:, 0] <= qx) & (data[:, 1] <= qy) # co-crash quadrant ax.axvspan(-8, qx, color=CRASH, alpha=0.06) ax.axhspan(-8, qy, color=CRASH, alpha=0.06) ax.scatter(data[~box, 0], data[~box, 1], s=6, c=col, alpha=0.25, edgecolors="none") ax.scatter(data[box, 0], data[box, 1], s=14, c=CRASH, alpha=0.7, edgecolors="none") ax.set_xlim(-6, 5) ax.set_ylim(-6, 5) ax.set_xlabel("asset A (z)") ax.set_ylabel("asset B (z)") ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=11) despine(ax) fig.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Regenerating the co-crash. Left: the real fat-tailed pair, lower-left co-crash quadrant shaded. Middle: RBIG-generated scenarios — the inverse map repacks the same lower-left corner, so its co-crash matches the real one. Right: a Gaussian Monte-Carlo with the identical correlation keeps the tilt but empties the corner, understating the joint tail. The fat-tail structure survives the backward map; it does not survive the Gaussian.](lab-jobC-scenarios_files/figure-html/fig-pair-cocrash-output-1.png){#fig-pair-cocrash width=1604 height=537} ::: ::: Two readings. First, the RBIG scenarios land on the real co-crash while the Gaussian undershoots it — the inverse map carried the fat joint tail across, which is the whole point of generating *through* a learned density rather than a covariance. Second, no new code did this: the same `fit_generate` from Rung 1, the same `cocrash_fraction`. Only the data got market-shaped. Now the real book. --- ## 📈 Rung 3 · Real — The Full Basket Now the real panel. We **reload** the prepared returns — there is no cleaning here. The full pipeline (turning prices into daily log-returns) and the co-crash structure these names ride on are worked out in [Co-Movement & Co-Crashes](../../data/04-co-movement-and-co-crashes.qmd); this lab just picks up that finished panel. We take a real sub-basket that spans two sectors — two banks and a big energy company, so there is a genuine cross-sector crash pattern to reproduce — and run the *same* `fit_generate`. **What we are looking for:** for each pair of names, the *co-crash fraction* — how often both names land in their worst 10% of days at the same time. We want the generated scenarios to show the same co-crash fractions as the real returns, which would mean the inverse map carried over the days when these names crash together. ::: {#fcc64fb1 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} R = datasets.load_returns() # prepared 14-name daily panel assets = ["JPM", "BAC", "XOM"] # two banks + one energy → cross-sector tail X_real: Float[Array, "n_days 3"] = R[assets].to_numpy() X_real = (X_real - X_real.mean(0)) / X_real.std(0) # z = (r − μ)/σ standardize each column print(f"{len(X_real)} trading days × {len(assets)} names " f"({R.index.min().date()} → {R.index.max().date()}) assets = {assets}") R[assets].head(3).round(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 4778 trading days × 3 names (2007-01-04 → 2025-12-30) assets = ['JPM', 'BAC', 'XOM'] ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ```{=html}

2007-01-08 0.0033 0.0039 -0.0081
``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note icon=false} ## Where This Data Comes From The panel, its sectors, and the co-crash structure these scenarios must reproduce are laid bare in the data primer — [Co-Movement & Co-Crashes](../../data/04-co-movement-and-co-crashes.qmd). This lab reloads that panel and never re-derives it. ::: Fitting RBIG takes a little time, so we keep the count modest — a few thousand generated scenarios is plenty for the tail statistics below. Same recipe, real data: ::: {#bd117181 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} gen_real: Float[Array, "n_gen 3"] = fit_generate(X_real, n_gen=4000, seed=0) print(f"generated {gen_real.shape[0]} three-asset scenarios from the real fit\n") print(f"{'pair':<12}{'real co-crash':>14}{'generated':>12}") print("-" * 38) for i, j in [(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 2)]: cr = cocrash_fraction(X_real[:, i], X_real[:, j]) cg = cocrash_fraction(gen_real[:, i], gen_real[:, j]) print(f"{assets[i] + '/' + assets[j]:<12}{cr:>14.0%}{cg:>12.0%}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` generated 4000 three-asset scenarios from the real fit pair real co-crash generated -------------------------------------- JPM/BAC 70% 70% JPM/XOM 42% 39% BAC/XOM 39% 38% ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-real-scenarios .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.6), sharex=True, sharey=True) for ax, data, col, ttl in [ (axL, X_real, COOL, f"real · co-crash {cocrash_fraction(X_real[:, 0], X_real[:, 1]):.0%}"), (axR, gen_real, WARM, f"generated · co-crash {cocrash_fraction(gen_real[:, 0], gen_real[:, 1]):.0%}"), ]: qx, qy = np.quantile(data[:, 0], 0.10), np.quantile(data[:, 1], 0.10) # 10% crash lines ax.axvspan(-8, qx, color=CRASH, alpha=0.06) ax.axhspan(-8, qy, color=CRASH, alpha=0.06) ax.scatter(data[:, 0], data[:, 1], s=7, c=col, alpha=0.3, edgecolors="none") ax.set_xlim(-6, 5) ax.set_ylim(-6, 5) ax.set_xlabel("JPM (z)") ax.set_ylabel("BAC (z)") ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=11) despine(ax) fig.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Real returns (left) and RBIG-generated scenarios (right) for the JPM/BAC pair from the three-asset fit. The bulk cloud and the shaded lower-left co-crash quadrant match — the within-bank joint crash the basket is famous for survives the backward map. The generator was fit on all three names jointly, so the cross-sector XOM tail is preserved too (see the table above).](lab-jobC-scenarios_files/figure-html/fig-real-scenarios-output-1.png){#fig-real-scenarios width=1304 height=537} ::: ::: The real basket behaves like the simplified pair, only messier: every pairwise co-crash in the generated set tracks the real one, including the cross-sector JPM/XOM tail — a bank and an energy name crashing together — that a simple correlation model would smooth away. The generator preserves the dangerous structure on data it was never told the structure of. --- ## 💰 Rung 4 · Application — The Stress Set The deliverable is a **stress set**: a batch of generated joint scenarios shipped with the tail statistics that justify trusting it. A stress set is only useful if it carries the *dangerous* structure, so we score it on exactly that and compare it to the real book using two numbers. The first is the **average pairwise co-crash fraction** — averaged over every pair of names, how often the two crash together. The second is the **worst-case joint loss** — imagine an equal-weight portfolio (the same amount in each name) and look at its single worst day; this is how deep that worst day goes. If the generator preserved the joint tail, both numbers should match the real data, and both should be larger than what a plain Gaussian simulation produces. ::: {#44359c65 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} def worst_joint_loss(data: Float[Array, "n d"]) -> float: """Most negative equal-weight portfolio return — the worst single day. p_t = (1/d) Σⱼ data[t, j] equal-weight book [z-score units] loss = min_t p_t the worst joint draw (a co-crash day) """ port: Float[Array, "n"] = einx.mean("t d -> t", data) # equal-weight daily return return float(port.min()) def mean_cocrash(data: Float[Array, "n d"]) -> float: """Average pairwise co-crash fraction over all asset pairs. mean_cocrash = (1 / |pairs|) Σ_(i14}{'worst joint loss':>18}") print("-" * 54) for name, data in [("real book", X_real), ("RBIG stress set", gen_real), ("Gaussian MC", g_real)]: print(f"{name:<22}{mean_cocrash(data):>14.0%}{worst_joint_loss(data):>18.2f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` source mean co-crash worst joint loss ------------------------------------------------------ real book 50% -7.57 RBIG stress set 49% -6.14 Gaussian MC 40% -2.77 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#fig-stress-set-compute .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Score each source on its danger: mean pairwise co-crash and the equal-weight loss tail. sources = [X_real, gen_real, g_real] # mean_cocrash = (1/|pairs|) Σ_(i t", s) for s in sources] ``` ::: ::: {#cell-fig-stress-set .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.6)) # Left: mean pairwise co-crash, three sources. names = ["real book", "RBIG\nstress set", "Gaussian\nMC"] cols = [COOL, WARM, "0.6"] axL.bar(names, [c * 100 for c in ccs], color=cols) axL.axhline(10, color=INK, lw=1.1, ls="--", label="independent baseline (10%)") axL.set_ylabel("mean pairwise co-crash (%)") axL.set_title("RBIG keeps the joint tail; the Gaussian thins it", fontsize=11) axL.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False) despine(axL) # Right: equal-weight portfolio-return distributions, tail in focus. bins = np.linspace(-5, 3, 60) for port, col, name in zip(ports, cols, ["real", "RBIG", "Gaussian"]): axR.hist(port, bins=bins, density=True, histtype="step", lw=1.8, color=col, label=name) axR.axvline(port.min(), color=col, lw=1.0, ls="--", alpha=0.8) # worst joint loss axR.set_xlim(-5, 3) axR.set_xlabel("equal-weight portfolio return (z)") axR.set_ylabel("density") axR.set_title("Portfolio loss tail — RBIG reaches the real worst case", fontsize=11) axR.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False) despine(axR) fig.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The stress set, scored on its danger. Left: average pairwise co-crash — the RBIG scenarios (orange) sit on the real book (blue) while the Gaussian Monte-Carlo (grey) falls short. Right: the distribution of equal-weight portfolio returns, left tail in focus; the RBIG tail reaches the real worst-case losses (dashed lines), the Gaussian tail stops short. The generator preserves the joint extremes a covariance-based sampler structurally misses.](lab-jobC-scenarios_files/figure-html/fig-stress-set-output-1.png){#fig-stress-set width=1425 height=537} ::: ::: The stress set passes its own test: its average co-crash and worst-case joint loss sit on the real book, while the Gaussian simulation — given the *exact* same correlations — understates both, because the joint extremes live in a fat tail that correlations alone cannot capture. These scenarios are the deliverable: a made-up batch that carries the real dangerous structure, ready to feed any portfolio risk function. Where this hands off: the uncertainty module takes a stress set like this one and turns it into risk figures — how much money the book could lose — see [Uncertainty · noise and propagation](../../uncertainty/03-noise-and-propagation.qmd).
